title: One in being
hook: the Son is of the same substance as the Father, the word said at Mass on Sundays

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicaea: bishops, some with burned hands and lost eyes, gathered to answer Arius. Your line was scarred bishops.

Sunday Mass, after the homily. The church stands and says the Creed together, and a few lines in comes a long, Latin-sounding word: consubstantial. It sounds like something from a chemistry class. Said in a breath, and the next line is already under way. That word is the answer the scarred bishops gave at Nicaea. Arius had said the Son was made. The council's reply is folded into this one clumsy, careful word.
screen: `SUNDAY, THE CREED.` → `A LONG, LATIN-SOUNDING WORD.` → `NICAEA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The bishops answered Arius with a Greek word: homoousios, of the same substance, the same being. The Catechism says the council at Nicaea confessed the Son as begotten, not made, of the same substance as the Father. In Latin that became consubstantialis; in English, consubstantial, or in older words, of one substance. The old Book of Common Prayer gives the creed's lines like this: "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made, Being of one substance with the Father." The Catholic Mass in English says it now as God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God. Same claim. Why did the bishops care so much? If the Son is a creature, however grand, then in Jesus God sent someone else. If the Son is of one being with the Father, then in Jesus God came himself. John's Gospel opens on exactly that: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And Jesus says in John, "I and the Father are one." Look at the creed's pictures. Light from light: a flame lit from a flame is not less fire than the first. Begotten, not made: a builder makes a house, something other than himself; a parent begets a child, someone of the same kind. Some readers notice the irony: a term from philosophy, chosen to guard what the bishops read in the Gospels. Clumsy on the tongue, and that is partly the point. It doesn't let the answer slide.
screen: `HOMOOUSIOS: OF THE SAME SUBSTANCE.` · `GOD SENT SOMEONE, OR CAME HIMSELF?` · `LIGHT FROM LIGHT.` · then, large: `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.` · then: `A WORD THAT DOESN'T LET IT SLIDE.`

segments.voice: If you know the Nicene Creed, say it quietly at half your usual speed and stop on the lines about the Son: God from God, Light from Light, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father. If you don't know it, rest on three words, breathing in on light and out on from light. If you pray, the creed itself is a prayer you can say.
Consubstantial. Of the same substance, one in being: the Son is not a creature, but God from God. Today's word.
Your line: god from god. One clumsy word, guarding a whole answer. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics say the Nicene Creed together at Mass on Sundays and solemnities, and the Roman Missal asks all to bow at the words about the Son becoming man.
